Question_text: A collector views a postage stamp of height 1.5cm through a lens. The lens is 2.0cm from the stamp. The image has a linear magnification of 3.0. The stamp, the image of the stamp and the position of the lens are shown full scale in Fig. 3.1. A ray of light from the top of the stamp to the lens is shown on Fig. 3.1.
image: Fig. 3.1 is a full-scale diagram on a grid, illustrating a lens, a stamp, and its image. A vertical object labeled 'stamp' is positioned to the left of a vertical line representing the 'position of lens'. A taller, inverted image, labeled 'image of stamp', is shown further to the left, implying it's a real image formed by a converging lens. The image appears larger than the object. A horizontal axis runs through the center of the lens. A single ray is shown originating from the top of the stamp, traveling towards the lens, and then passing through it, continuing on the other side. A small arrow indicates '1 cm' for scale on the grid. A label 'image viewed from this side of the lens' points to the right side of the lens, and the image itself is shown on the left of the lens.

State what is meant by linear magnification.

Question_text: A teacher demonstrates magnetic screening. When a magnet is placed near a small cardboard box, paper clips on the other side of the box are picked up, as shown in Fig. 4.1. When a small piece of soft iron is placed inside the box as shown in Fig. 4.2, the paper clips fall off. Magnetic field lines in each diagram are shown as thin lines.
image: Fig. 4.1 and Fig. 4.2 illustrate magnetic screening. Fig. 4.1 shows a U-shaped magnet with North (N) and South (S) poles. A cardboard box is placed between the poles, and magnetic field lines are drawn passing through the box. Paper clips are shown clinging to the outside of the box, indicating the magnetic field penetrates it. Fig. 4.2 shows a similar setup, but with a piece of 'soft iron' placed inside the cardboard box. In this case, the magnetic field lines appear to be concentrated within the soft iron, and the paper clips previously clinging to the outside of the box are now fallen off, indicating the soft iron has screened the area outside the box from the magnetic field.

Parts.part_text: On Fig. 4.1, mark an arrow on each of the magnetic field lines to show its direction.
Explain why placing the soft iron inside the box causes the paper clips to fall off.
Explain why it is sensible to have magnetic screening around the tube of a cathode-ray oscilloscope.

Question_text: Fig. 6.1 shows a coil of wire connected by flexible leads to a switch and a battery. The coil is placed between the poles of a permanent magnet and is free to turn about the axis. When the switch is closed, forces due to the current act on the sides of the coil. The coil starts to turn.
image: Fig. 6.1 illustrates a simple DC motor setup. A rectangular coil of wire, labeled 'coil', is positioned between the North (N) and South (S) poles of a permanent magnet. The coil is connected by 'flexible leads' to a switch and a battery. An 'axis' is indicated, around which the coil is free to rotate. The flexible leads connect to a split-ring commutator (not explicitly labeled as such in the main diagram, but implied by the circuit and the mention in part c) which contacts carbon brushes.

Parts.part_text: On Fig. 6.1, draw arrows to show the directions of the forces.

In order for the coil to rotate continuously, a split-ring commutator is connected between the battery and the coil. Explain how the split-ring commutator enables the coil to rotate continuously. Include a diagram in your answer.
